EXHIBIT 4
AFFIDAVIT OF STEVEN HERLING

1 
 
I. 
QUALIFICATIONS AND PURPOSE OF AFFIDAVIT 
 
1. 
My name is Steven R. Herling.  I am currently President of Herling Power Grid 
Consulting, Inc. (“HPGC”), which provides consulting services related to planning, operational, 
and regulatory issues facing the electric power industry. My business address is 513 William 
Salesbury Drive, Downingtown, PA 19335. Through HPGC, I have served as a subcontractor to 
other consulting firms, such as The Brattle Group and Charles River Associates, advising on 
projects related to off-shore wind development and utility investment opportunities. I have also 
advised clients on generator and merchant transmission interconnection issues as well as a range 
of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) 
process issues. 
2. 
In July 2020, I retired from PJM, where I had been employed since May 1990. At PJM, I 
held a number of positions in the Operations and Planning Divisions and was promoted to Vice 
President of Planning in May 2004. While at PJM, I contributed to or led initiatives that resulted 
in a wide range of milestone achievements in PJM’s evolution and growth as a regional 
transmission organization (“RTO”), including the creation of the RTEP process, the development 
of procedures and standard terms and conditions for generation and merchant transmission 
interconnections, the development of the competitive transmission process, and the reliability 
and resource adequacy aspects of successive integrations of additional control areas that more 
than doubled the size of the PJM market area. In addition to my work for PJM, I contributed to a 
wide range of activities for the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) and 
served on various regional industry working groups and committees addressing reliability and 
planning matters.

2 
3.
Prior to PJM, I worked for the General Public Utilities Service Corporation (“GPU”) for
three years in systems operations, where I was responsible for dispatcher training and 
certification, operations and planning activities, and energy management system and operational 
support tools. Prior to GPU, I worked for the American Electric Power Service Corporation 
(“AEP”) for eight years in bulk transmission planning. In that position, I performed a range of 
power system analyses related to the AEP 765 kV transmission system, generator and circuit 
breaker dynamic modeling, and the mechanical behavior of turbine-generator shaft systems. 
4.
I hold a Bachelor of Science in Electric Power Engineering and a Master of Engineering
in Electric Power Engineering, both from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.1 
5.
I have testified on a number of occasions in proceedings before the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (“FERC”), as well as various state commissions and legislative task 
forces, on matters relating to system planning and reliability issues.  I have also testified in 
transmission line Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (“CPCN”) proceedings in 
Pennsylvania, Maryland, West Virginia, Virginia, and New Jersey, and I have testified in a 
transfer of ownership case for a public utility in Kentucky. 
6.
I have been asked by Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) to provide
an affidavit that discusses, from an engineering perspective, transmission and related services 
taken by load under the PJM Tariff for a range of co-located load configurations based on the 
options discussed in the Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. filed on March 24, 2025, in the 
above-captioned consolidated proceedings (“PJM Answer”). The PJM options range from load 
connected to the grid, separate from any generating resources, to a variety of co-location 
configurations. This affidavit and the opinions expressed herein are based on my experience in 
1 Please refer to my resume attached as Attachment A.

3 
 
the field of electric power system planning, operation, and regulation and my knowledge of the 
electric power industry. My opinions and analyses are subject to change if additional information 
becomes available. 
7. 
My affidavit will describe eight possible configurations of large co-located load projects, 
identified by PJM as Option 1 through Option 8, to provide an engineering basis for a discussion 
of the transmission and related services taken, or not taken, by co-located loads. For each 
configuration, I will discuss the extent to which the configuration imposes incremental burden on 
the PJM system with respect to the services and the circumstances under which the co-located 
load takes service. My conclusions are further summarized at the end of the affidavit. 
II. 
DESCRIPTION OF CO-LOCATION PROJECT OPTIONS 
 
8. 
As a general matter, co-located loads rely on direct connection to co-located generation 
facilities for the delivery of energy without reliance on grid transmission facilities or Network 
Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”).   
9. 
A number of the PJM options, however, contemplate continued connection of the load to 
the grid, even following the loss of the co-located generating facility. These include PJM Options 
1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8. In those cases, the co-located load will rely on the grid and NITS for energy.  
10. 
In contrast, in PJM Option 4, the co-located load will not be able to draw energy from the 
grid. Instead, fully redundant relaying will trip the co-located load in the event of (i) the 
unplanned loss of the co-located generation or (ii) a reduction in generation level, thereby 
preventing the co-located load from being able to draw energy from the grid.  In such 
configurations, no energy will flow under any circumstances from the co-located generation 
facilities over grid transmission to the co-located load and, therefore, no grid transmission 
service is used by or required by the co-located load. The same fully redundant relaying is true of

4 
 
PJM Option 5 with the limited exception of the load taking back-up service, if permitted by PJM, 
following the loss of the co-located generation resource, from generating resources to which it is 
not directly connected. 
PJM Options: 
11. 
PJM’s Option 1 is based on load connected to the grid at a separate Point of 
Interconnection from any generator. The load is Network Load and any generator that might be 
contractually serving the load is a capacity resource. The load and generation may be physically 
located at the same location, but they are electrically connected to the grid, separately, and not 
electrically co-located. 
12. 
PJM’s Option 2 is based on co-located load and generation connected to the grid at the 
same Point of Interconnection, but separately metered. The load is Network Load and the 
generator is a capacity resource. While physically co-located at the same Point of 
Interconnection, Option 2 treats the load and generator as separate entities with respect to all 
services, regardless of any bilateral arrangements that may exist.   
13. 
PJM’s Option 3 is based on the existing Behind the Meter Generation (“BTMG”) 
construct, where load is the primary customer, netting with a co-located generator at the same 
Point of Interconnection.  Electrically, the physical connection of load and generation behind the 
same Point of Interconnection is the same in Option 3 as in Option 2. The load is Network Load 
when it consumes energy in excess of what the co-located generator produces, and the portion of 
the generator designated as BTMG is not a capacity resource.  
14. 
PJM’s Option 4 is based on co-located load and generation connected to the grid at the 
same Point of Interconnection. The load is located behind the generator with protection 
mechanisms in place to prevent the delivery of energy from the grid to serve the load when the

associated generator is out of service. The load is not Network Load, and the portion of the 
generator committed to the load is not a capacity resource. 
15. 
I include Figure 1 as a sample design to illustrate such a co-located load configuration 
associated with a nuclear generating facility with two generating units.  In Figure 1, the co-
located load is served at 34.5 kV on a number of new buses, connected, behind-the-meter, by 
multiple transformers stepping down from generator step-up transformer high-side voltages to 
34.5 kV. The co-located load can be served from either one of the generating units or split and 
served by the two units.    
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 1 - One-Line Diagram of a Sample Co-Located Load Project Incorporating Redundant Relaying to 
Facilitate Disconnection from the Grid During Generation Outages

6 
 
16. 
As a point of reference, Constellation has previously submitted co-located load projects 
similar in configuration and design to PJM’s Option 4 or Option 5 to PJM for evaluation through 
Necessary Studies, as provided for in the PJM Tariff, to determine whether planned 
modifications will have a permanent material impact on the transmission system and to identify 
the additions, modifications, or replacements to the transmission system, if any, that are 
necessary. 
17. 
PJM’s Option 5 is the same as Option 4 from a configuration perspective, including 
protection mechanisms, but allows for back-up service to be provided to the load from the PJM 
grid. Under PJM’s description, such back-up service would only be provided with PJM’s 
approval and such approval could be denied or withdrawn by PJM based on system conditions.   
18. 
Option 6 is similar to Option 2, except that under PJM’s proposal the new load brings 
new generation to the grid with which it will be co-located to obtain the opportunity for faster 
interconnection. The new load does not include the type of special protection relay scheme 
envisioned in Option 4. 
19. 
PJM’s Option 7 is similar to Option 2, except that the service received by the load will be 
interruptible. The status of the generator does not change, i.e., the generator can remain a 
capacity resource. The load receiving interruptible service is separately metered but does not 
include the type of special protection relay scheme envisioned in Option 4.  
20. 
PJM’s Option 8 is similar to Option 2, but provides the opportunity for the co-located 
load to participate in an expanded form of Demand Response. 
III. 
PROTECTIVE RELAY SCHEMES 
21. 
As discussed, Options 4 and 5 will require protective relay schemes that will prevent load 
from drawing energy from the grid. These protective relay schemes can be designed so that there 
are completely redundant primary and backup protective schemes to perform this function.

7 
 
22. 
Such a configuration uses electric current transformers to measure the flow of power 
from between the co-located load and the grid, which is communicated with relays via fiber optic 
channels that will trip behind-the-meter circuit breakers associated with the co-located load when 
the electric current transformers sense the power flow from the grid to the co-located load. This 
can occur in the event of the sudden loss of the co-located generating unit or following a 
reduction in the level of energy produced by the co-located generating unit so that it is not fully 
supplying the co-located load.  There are two circuit breakers placed in series supplying the co-
located load, so that if one fails, the second will still open the circuit. Each circuit breaker has 
two trip coils such that either the primary or backup protective relay can successfully trip the 
load. All elements of the protective scheme, including the electric current transformers, the fiber 
channels, and the trip relays, are redundant resulting in a single-failure-proof design.  The 
protective scheme referred to above in Figure 1 will trip the co-located load from the grid in 
three cycles (0.05 seconds) following a trip of the co-located generating unit or after sensing that 
the energy produced by the co-located generating unit has been reduced to a level such that the 
co-located load is attempting to draw energy from the grid. 
23. 
PJM raises the concern that “[t]he challenge with an arrangement where there is load 
located behind a generator Point of Interconnection lies in how such a configuration or special 
protection scheme could be designed to never fail . . . .”2  PJM plans for N-1 conditions followed 
by a single protection system failure, such as a stuck breaker, and requires transmission system 
upgrades when such events result in violations of applicable NERC standards. In this instance, a 
stuck breaker becomes a second contingency. In most instances, the solution to stuck breaker 
criteria violations is to add a redundant series breaker, making the failure of both breakers 
 
2 PJM Answer at 44.

8 
 
following an N-1 event a third contingency. PJM does not plan for or require upgrades for such 
third contingencies, nor would it be reasonable to do so, short of events that would result in a 
cascading outage of grid facilities. The protection system, discussed above, is fully redundant 
and, while it cannot be guaranteed to never fail, it is unreasonable to treat the failure of both 
primary and secondary relay system facilities following the loss of a generator as anything other 
than a third contingency.  In fact, when I was directing transmission planning for PJM, I cannot 
think of an instance in which we treated such a situation otherwise.  In practice, protection 
schemes are regularly employed on the PJM transmission system, and the successful operation of 
such protective systems is a common observance within PJM.  There is no technical reason from 
my perspective to expect that protective relaying in the context of co-location would perform any 
less reliably.  If anything, suggesting that protective relaying – a common and technically sound 
tool for managing the grid – cannot be used in the context of co-located configurations or must 
be designed to a different standard strikes me as an unduly discriminatory position.  
IV. 
GRID SERVICES 
24. 
With the different technical configurations for co-located load in mind, I discuss below 
the various transmission and related services and the extent to which the co-located load imposes 
incremental burden on the PJM system with respect to the services it takes or does not take.  
a. Network Integration Transmission Service 
25. 
NITS is the means by which Network Load in the PJM region is served over the PJM 
transmission system, utilizing identified Network Resources as well as other non-designated 
generation resources.3 The PJM RTEP ensures the on-going reliability and ability of the PJM 
transmission system to provide service to load customers via NITS and long-term firm point-to-
 
3 PJM Tariff, Part III, Sections 28.1 and 28.3.

9 
 
point transmission service. Transmission facilities necessary to connect new load customers to 
the grid are identified and integrated into the RTEP to ensure the integrity of the models used in 
analyses and the on-going reliability of service to all customers.  
26. 
In PJM’s Option 1, a new Network Load would be fully dependent on NITS for delivery 
of capacity and energy, would be included in the PJM load forecast, and would be modeled and 
planned for in future RTEP cycles. This is the manner in which the vast majority of load is 
connected to the PJM grid. 
27. 
In PJM’s Option 2, a new load and the co-located generator are separately metered. The 
load is considered Network Load and the generator is a capacity resource. While energy will 
flow directly from the generator (when it is in service) to the load without flowing over the 
facilities of the PJM grid, the load would be dependent on NITS for delivery of capacity and 
energy at some times, would be included in the PJM load forecast, and would be modeled and 
planned for in future RTEP cycles. The dependence of the load on NITS covers all 
circumstances, whether the generator is in or out of service.  
28. 
PJM’s Option 3 is based on the existing BTMG construct and can involve two 
configurations where load and generation can be co-located or connected via the distribution 
system of a municipal utility.  The existing PJM Tariff bills for transmission and related services 
based on the netting of such load with its BTMG.  
29. 
In PJM’s Option 4, a new load is co-located behind a generating resource. As shown in 
Figure 1 above, the connection is radial, behind the Point of Interconnection of the generator. 
Therefore, energy can only flow directly from the co-located generator’s grid voltage substations 
to the behind-the-meter co-location project’s substations (at the same grid voltage level) and, 
from there, over step-down transformers to the co-located load connected at 34.5 kV. There is no

10 
 
other transmission path from the co-located generation to the co-located load, i.e., there is no 
parallel path for energy to flow out from the co-located generator onto the transmission grid and 
back, eventually, to the co-located load.  Because the associated special-purpose relay scheme 
will remove the co-located load from the grid in the event of a sudden loss of the generating 
facility, no energy will flow to the co-located load over the transmission grid following a 
contingency; no new transmission infrastructure will be required on the grid to facilitate the 
interconnection and to ensure reliability for existing load customers other than what might be 
identified in the Necessary Study performed to determine whether the generator’s modification 
to serve the behind-the-meter load has any reliability impact, and no NITS service will be 
provided by the grid to the co-located load. Excess energy, beyond the level required by the load, 
will flow from the generator to the grid. Accordingly, the load is not dependent on NITS for 
delivery of capacity and energy, would not be included in the PJM load forecast, and would not 
be modeled and planned for in future RTEP cycles. 
30. 
In PJM’s Option 5, a new load is co-located behind a generating resource in the same 
manner as Option 4. As shown in Figure 1 above, the connection is radial, behind the Point of 
Interconnection of the generator and, therefore, energy is delivered from the generator directly to 
the load without flowing on any grid transmission facilities. Excess energy, beyond the level 
required by the load, will flow from the generator to the grid. Protection mechanisms are in place 
to prevent the delivery of energy from the grid to the load in the event that the generator is 
offline. The significant difference with Option 5 is that the load can take back-up service from 
PJM with advance authorization. The load is not dependent on NITS for delivery of capacity and 
energy while the primary generation source is in service, but may rely on transmission facilities 
of the PJM grid for back-up service, depending on the electrical location of the back-up

11 
 
generation source. To the extent that back-up service is supplied by a second generating resource 
at the same electrical location, energy from that resource would also not flow on any grid 
transmission facilities. 
31. 
With respect to PJM Option 4 and PJM Option 5, PJM notes that co-location 
arrangements may involve the sale of power from generators to intermediaries and then to load 
under certain circumstances.4 This, however, is a contractual difference, not a physical, 
electrical, or interconnection design-based difference. The delivery of energy from generation to 
load in co-location arrangements such as PJM’s Option 4 and Option 5 does not involve the flow 
of that energy over the transmission facilities of the grid. This fact is a function of the design of 
the interconnection between the co-located load and generation and is not impacted by the 
ownership of the generation facility or the co-located load or any contractual relationship 
between those parties. BTMG arrangements and co-located load arrangements can be designed 
from an engineering perspective in exactly the same manner. In one, the load is typically greater 
in magnitude than the generating facility. In the other, the load is typically lesser in magnitude 
than the generating facility. The physics of energy delivery are the same in both arrangements 
and are not related to contractual arrangements or rate structures.  
32. 
Finally, Option 7 contemplates the ability to curtail load in advance of 
emergency conditions. While not specifically a co-location configuration feature, this contractual 
arrangement can provide a valuable tool to PJM operators with which to manage operational 
emergencies. It could be implemented as a transitional service while required transmission 
system upgrades are under construction.  
 
4 PJM Answer at 25.

12 
 
b. Synchronization 
33. 
Comparing PJM’s Option 4 and PJM’s Option 5 with the BTMG construct (the basis for 
PJM Option 3), clearly both arrangements involve load and generation that is synchronized to the 
grid. However, synchronization does not require or suggest that energy delivery from that 
generation to that load flows on the transmission facilities of the grid. Synchronization is clearly 
important and even necessary to the stability of the generating facility and the ability of the 
generating facility to deliver energy to the co-located load on an on-going basis, but that does not 
change the fact that the energy does not flow on the transmission facilities of the grid.  
34. 
Whether synchronization could be conceptualized and designated as an ancillary service, 
one thing is clear: it is not an ancillary service within PJM. The ability to provide other ancillary 
services, if they are required or used, is facilitated by synchronization, but one is not the 
equivalent of the other. Synchronization may allow black start service to be provided, but if 
black start service is not required or used by a co-located load, the fact that the load is 
synchronized to the grid does not make the service required or used. In response to question 
b.vi., PJM states that “[s]ynchronizing to the grid means the generator matches the voltage, 
frequency, and phase of the entire grid (including all load connected to the system) before 
connecting to the grid in order to facilitate safe and stable power transfer. As noted above, co-
located load is connected to and synchronized with the multi-state bulk power system. At bare 
minimum, it is benefiting from ancillary services.”5 Load benefits from being synchronized to 
the grid, but not from services that it does not use. One standard on which charges for grid 
services can be properly based is use of those services. This applies to both transmission service 
and ancillary services. Synchronization, alone, should not be the standard for such charges.  
 
5 Id. at 43.

13 
 
c. Other Grid Services 
I have previously analyzed grid services in connection with a co-located load 
configuration that, while synchronized to the grid, provides for disconnection from the grid when 
the co-located generation facility is unavailable.  In short, my prior analysis shows that co-
located load configurations that include sufficiently redundant protective relay systems, e.g., 
configurations consistent with PJM’s Options 4 and 5, prevent the physical flow of power to the 
co-located load and do not use transmission service from the grid.6  Moreover, my prior analysis 
shows that these configurations do not impose burdens on the PJM system that would require the 
procurement of additional amounts of ancillary services.7  
35. 
Further, the PJM Tariff, which establishes the procedures for calculating charges for 
services provided in PJM markets, dictates for all of the services discussed herein, that the 
obligation of a behind-the-meter co-located load is based on the amount of such load, netted by 
the generation that is operating behind-the-meter.    
36. 
My presentation here is an engineering analysis that, among other things, considers 
whether non-grid connected co-location configurations consistent with PJM Options 4 and 5 
impose additional burdens on the PJM grid.  I note that I do not take a position here, nor did I in 
my prior analysis, whether the co-located load under the non-grid connected configurations of 
PJM Options 4 and 5 may nevertheless benefit indirectly by virtue of synchronization through 
the host generator’s interconnection to the grid. To date, however, FERC has not allocated 
charges for any such synchronization benefits. 
37. 
This concludes my affidavit. 
 
6 Protest of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC to the Exelon Companies’ Rate Filings, Docket Nos. ER24-2888-
000, et al., Att. 1, Affidavit of Steven R. Herling at ¶¶ 14-34 (Oct. 2, 2024).  
7 Id.

VERIFICATION 
I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing Affidavit is true and correct to the best of 
my knowledge, information, and belief.  
Executed this 23rd day of April 2025. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
________________________ 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Steven R. Herling
